A five-condition controlled design reveals these mechanisms separately, showing aggregate pipeline safety is not stable, raw-direct rankings mispredict deployed behavior, and evaluations should report each factor independently.
AI.motivation: Current safety evaluations of multi-agent LLM systems aggregate the difference between direct prompts and planner-executor pipelines as a single "pipeline effect," which conflates multiple mechanisms (reframing harmful intent as operational work, planner refusal/transformation, and executor delegation effects), making the aggregate difficult to interpret.
AI.method: A five-condition controlled contrast design evaluated on 30 synthetic harmful scenarios plus an external validation set from four agent-safety benchmarks, using LLM-judged compliance to separate the three mechanisms (operational reframing, planner behavior, delegation framing).
AI.result: Operational reframing is the most portable risk signal (increases compliance for GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek; Claude resistant). Planner behavior offsets risk mainly via refusal, but when executable steps are produced, executor compliance can exceed the direct operational baseline. Raw-direct model rankings mispredict: Gemini is safest under raw-direct but shows largest amplification with a Claude planner (8.9%→38.9%); GPT's near-zero aggregate pipeline effect hides reframing increase canceled by planner refusal.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent safety evaluations should report reframing, planner behavior, delegation framing, and model pairing separately before attributing failures to architecture itself.

title: Ace! Motion Planning of Professional-Level Table Tennis Serves with a Robot Arm
summary: Table tennis, a dynamic, compact, and popular sport, has received significant attention as a robotics benchmark over the last decades. Most of the research has focused on the rally aspect - returning an incoming ball - requiring high-speed vision, agile motion planning, and tight closed-loop control. However, the other component of table tennis gameplay - the serve - is comparatively a quite unexplored research problem, that in fact requires pushing physics modeling and control to the extremes. Achieving competitive serves with a robot presents domain-specific challenges, such as high-spin generation from a spinless ball, precise aiming, or multi-objective optimization. In this work, we present a novel approach for generating official rule-compliant serves by combining motion primitives, Model Predictive Control, and Bayesian Optimization. Serves generated in this way offer a wide and controllable variation of spins of up to 550 rad/s, and speeds of up to 6.7 m/s, matching and even surpassing those of elite table tennis players.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel robotic approach for generating rule-compliant table tennis serves by combining motion primitives, Model Predictive Control, and Bayesian Optimization, achieving spins up to 550 rad/s and speeds up to 6.7 m/s that match or surpass elite human players.
AI.motivation: While robotic table tennis rallying has been extensively studied, the serve component remains largely unexplored despite requiring extreme physics modeling, control, and domain-specific challenges such as high-spin generation from a spinless ball, precise aiming, and multi-objective optimization.
AI.method: The approach combines motion primitives, Model Predictive Control (MPC), and Bayesian Optimization to generate official rule-compliant table tennis serves.
AI.result: The system generates serves with wide and controllable variation of spins up to 550 rad/s and speeds up to 6.7 m/s, matching and even surpassing elite table tennis players.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method successfully addresses the unexplored robotic table tennis serve problem, pushing physics modeling and control to achieve competitive, rule-compliant serves with elite-level performance metrics.

title: Does AI Understand Imaging? A Systematic Benchmark of Agentic AI for Computational Imaging Tasks
comment: 14 pages, 11 figures. Preprint / work in progress. Paper Webpage: https://cirp-lab.github.io/imagingbench
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) and agentic AI have shown strong performance on semantic visual tasks, but it remains unclear whether they can handle the physics and inverse problems that underlie computational imaging. We present ImagingBench, a benchmark of 20 computational imaging tasks spanning five categories: ray and wave optics, image signal processing, inverse reconstruction, computational sensing, and calibration. ImagingBench evaluates three complementary settings: Expert, fixed expert-guided inverse reconstruction; Planner, planner-guided inverse reconstruction; and Forward, forward-system simulation for consistency checking. We benchmark leading proprietary and open-source image-centric multimodal systems, including Gemini, GPT, and Qwen, and compare them with representative task-specific non-agentic baselines. Across tasks, agentic models remain consistently weaker than specialized methods, especially on computational sensing problems such as lensless imaging, event-based reconstruction, time-of-flight imaging, and holography. Planner guidance provides only modest and inconsistent gains over the fixed-prompt Expert baseline. Although the models often generate visually plausible outputs, their reference-based fidelity remains poor, revealing a substantial gap between semantic visual competence and physically grounded imaging performance. ImagingBench provides a unified testbed for measuring this gap and tracking progress in agentic AI for computational imaging.

AI.tldr: ImagingBench is a benchmark of 20 computational imaging tasks evaluating VLMs and agentic AI across three settings (Expert, Planner, Forward). Results show agentic models significantly underperform specialized methods, especially on sensing problems, and reveal a large gap between semantic visual competence and physically grounded imaging performance.
AI.motivation: To assess whether VLMs and agentic AI systems, which excel at semantic visual tasks, can handle the physics and inverse problems fundamental to computational imaging—an area not previously benchmarked.
AI.method: Constructed ImagingBench with 20 tasks across 5 categories (ray/wave optics, ISP, inverse reconstruction, computational sensing, calibration). Evaluated models under three settings: Expert (fixed expert-guided inverse reconstruction), Planner (planner-guided inverse reconstruction), and Forward (forward simulation for consistency). Benchmarked Gemini, GPT, Qwen and compared with task-specific non-agentic baselines.
AI.result: Agentic models consistently underperform specialized methods, particularly on computational sensing tasks (lensless imaging, event-based reconstruction, ToF imaging, holography). Planner guidance yields only modest/inconsistent gains over fixed Expert prompts. Models produce visually plausible outputs but have poor reference-based fidelity.
AI.conclusion: There is a substantial gap between semantic visual competence and physically grounded imaging performance in current VLMs/agentic AI. ImagingBench provides a unified testbed to measure this gap and track future progress.

title: A Closed-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Robust Multi-Robot Manipulation
summary: Multi-robot systems provide the parallelism and redundancy necessary for long-horizon tasks, while Large Language Models (LLMs) offer the reasoning capabilities to decompose these objectives into actionable plans. However, effectively grounding this high-level reasoning in physical multi-robot execution remains an open challenge. Existing LLM-based approaches fall mainly into two categories: Single-robot methods achieve robust contact-rich manipulation but lack the coordination mechanisms required for tasks spanning multiple workspaces. Current multi-robot frameworks focus on high-level planning, often treating manipulation as an idealized primitive that fails to account for real-world execution uncertainties. To address this, we propose a hierarchical closed-loop agentic LLM-based framework to ensure robust multi-robot manipulation. Our system consists of three specialized agents: the Planning Agent decomposes instructions into allocated sub-tasks, the Manipulation Agent for each robot executes actions via adaptive tool use, and the Verification Agent closes the loop by monitoring physical outcomes and feeding back semantic corrections. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves superior success rates, ensures robust adaptability ranging from single to cross workspace manipulation, and offers a generalizable approach for diverse manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical closed-loop LLM-based framework with three specialized agents (Planning, Manipulation, Verification) enables robust multi-robot manipulation across single and cross workspaces, achieving superior success rates and generalizability in real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-robot methods either lack coordination (single-robot) or treat manipulation as an idealized primitive ignoring execution uncertainties (multi-robot), leaving a gap in grounding high-level reasoning in physical multi-robot execution.
AI.method: A hierarchical closed-loop agentic LLM-based framework with three agents: Planning Agent (decomposes instructions into sub-tasks), Manipulation Agent (per-robot adaptive tool-use execution), and Verification Agent (monitors physical outcomes and provides semantic corrections to close the loop).
AI.result: Real-world experiments show superior success rates, robust adaptability from single to cross workspace manipulation, and generalizability across diverse manipulation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hierarchical closed-loop framework effectively bridges LLM reasoning with physical multi-robot execution, addressing coordination and uncertainty challenges for robust manipulation.

title: Reasoning Consistency Scanning: A Framework for Auditing Chain-of-Thought Validity in AI Safety Evaluations
summary: Prior work has shown that chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is often unfaithful: a model's stated reasoning does not reliably reflect the process that produced its output. Detecting unfaithfulness, though, requires controlled experimental interventions, which cannot be applied to evaluation transcripts after the fact. We turn instead to a more tractable question that has received less attention: whether the stated reasoning is logically consistent with the answer it accompanies. Unlike faithfulness, consistency can be assessed from a transcript alone, with no intervention. We introduce reasoning consistency scanning, a reusable method for detecting this property in AI safety evaluation transcripts. Our contributions are fourfold. First, we formalize reasoning consistency as distinct from faithfulness and define a six-subtype taxonomy of inconsistency. Second, we build a validated benchmark of 60 transcripts, manually adapted from InstrumentalEval outputs. Third, we implement a working scanner for InspectScout, the first to target this property in safety evaluation transcripts. Fourth, we report results across four generator models and three evaluations from inspect_evals, showing that reasoning inconsistency is present, detectable, and varies systematically across both models and task types.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces reasoning consistency scanning, a method to detect whether a model's stated chain-of-thought reasoning is logically consistent with its final answer, distinguishing this from the harder problem of measuring faithfulness. The authors formalize a six-subtype taxonomy of inconsistency, build a validated benchmark of 60 transcripts, implement a working scanner for InspectScout, and show across four models and three evaluations that inconsistency is present, detectable, and varies systematically.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows chain-of-thought reasoning is often unfaithful, but detecting unfaithfulness requires controlled interventions that cannot be applied post-hoc. The authors turn to a more tractable question—whether stated reasoning is logically consistent with the answer—since consistency can be assessed from a transcript alone without intervention.
AI.method: The authors formalize reasoning consistency as distinct from faithfulness, define a six-subtype taxonomy of inconsistency, build a validated benchmark of 60 transcripts manually adapted from InstrumentalEval outputs, implement a working scanner for InspectScout, and evaluate across four generator models and three evaluations from inspect_evals.
AI.result: The scanner detects reasoning inconsistency in safety evaluation transcripts. Inconsistency is present, detectable, and varies systematically across both models and task types.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning inconsistency is a tractable and detectable property that can be assessed from transcripts alone, offering a practical approach for auditing chain-of-thought reasoning in safety evaluations without requiring experimental interventions.

title: PriGo: Test-Time Primitive Guidance to Diffusion and Flow Policies for Adaptive Robotic Manipulation
summary: Imitation learning has enabled remarkable progress in robotic manipulation, especially with diffusion and flow-based policies that generate complex visuomotor behaviors directly from demonstrations. Yet, despite their strong performance, these policies often fail to generalize across tasks and environments. A key reason is that existing policies tend to imitate superficial action correlations rather than the underlying intent. Inspired by the compositional structure of human behaviors, we propose PriGo, a primitive-guided test-time adaptive framework for robust robotic manipulation. PriGo introduces PANet, a lightweight primitive prediction module that infers primitive distributions directly from observations. We further propose a differentiable primitive guidance mechanism that refines generated actions during inference, steering trajectories toward semantically consistent behaviors. Unlike prior primitive-conditioned approaches, PriGo operates entirely at test time and can be seamlessly integrated into pretrained diffusion and flow policies without retraining. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, CALVIN, SIMPLER, and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that PriGo consistently improves robustness, long-horizon execution, and generalization ability across both diffusion and flow-based policies.

AI.tldr: PriGo is a primitive-guided test-time adaptive framework that improves robustness, long-horizon execution, and generalization of pretrained diffusion and flow-based robotic manipulation policies by inferring primitive distributions and refining actions during inference without retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing imitation learning policies for robotic manipulation often fail to generalize across tasks and environments because they imitate superficial action correlations rather than underlying intent.
AI.method: PriGo introduces PANet (a lightweight primitive prediction module) and a differentiable primitive guidance mechanism that refines generated actions during inference to steer trajectories toward semantically consistent behaviors, operating entirely at test time without retraining.
AI.result: Experiments on LIBERO, CALVIN, SIMPLER, and real-world robotic tasks show consistent improvements in robustness, long-horizon execution, and generalization across both diffusion and flow-based policies.
AI.conclusion: PriGo effectively bridges the gap between primitive-conditioned approaches and test-time adaptation, offering a plug-and-play solution to enhance generalization in imitation learning for robotic manipulation.

title: From Atomic Actions to Standard Operating Procedures: Iterative Tool Optimization for Self-Evolving LLM Agents
summary: Tool utilization enables Large Language Model (LLM) agents to interact with the real world and resolve complex tasks. However, existing agent frameworks predominantly rely on static toolsets composed of granular atomic actions (e.g., basic file I/O or single-turn search), which forces agents to reinvent low-level logic for every recurring workflow, leading to increased reasoning overhead and failure rates. In this study, we propose that agents can achieve self-evolution by synthesizing these atomic actions into reusable Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), which function as callable higher-order tools that encapsulate multi-step logic. We further introduce EvoSOP, a framework that empowers agents to extract SOPs from execution trajectories and iteratively optimize the toolset through a systematic lifecycle of construction, merging, evaluation, and pruning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EvoSOP significantly boosts task success rates while substantially reducing the number of interaction rounds compared to baselines. Our analysis also reveals that iterative tool optimization fosters reliable and efficient tool-use patterns, providing a scalable pathway for the development of self-evolving agents.

AI.tldr: EvoSOP enables LLM agents to self-evolve by synthesizing atomic actions into reusable Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), significantly improving task success rates and reducing interaction rounds.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent frameworks rely on static, atomic toolsets (e.g., basic file I/O, single-turn search), forcing agents to reinvent low-level logic for recurring workflows, increasing reasoning overhead and failure rates.
AI.method: EvoSOP framework extracts SOPs (callable higher-order tools encapsulating multi-step logic) from execution trajectories, and iteratively optimizes the toolset through a lifecycle of construction, merging, evaluation, and pruning.
AI.result: EvoSOP significantly boosts task success rates and substantially reduces the number of interaction rounds compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Iterative tool optimization fosters reliable and efficient tool-use patterns, providing a scalable pathway for developing self-evolving agents.

title: GeoProp: Grounding Robot State in Vision for Generalist Manipulation
summary: Proprioception is fundamental to robotic manipulation, yet standard fusion methods often treat it as an isolated vector lacking explicit alignment with visual tokens. Without a direct correspondence between 3D kinematics and 2D feature maps, manipulation policies struggle to ground the robot's state within the scene, frequently underperforming even vision-only baselines. To address this, we introduce GeoProp, a lightweight, plug-and-play adapter that aligns proprioception with vision through explicit geometric grounding and spatial feature sampling. GeoProp projects the robot state onto the image plane to sample localized visual features, constructing a grounded state token. It then injects state-derived spatial priors into the corresponding visual features via FiLM modulation. To capture motion intent, GeoProp further samples features at a short-horizon predicted coordinate derived from recent kinematics, providing look-ahead visual context. Across 67 tasks, GeoProp improves Diffusion Policy by 8.7% on 63 simulation tasks and pi_0 by 4.0% on the RoboTwin subset, and yields a 10.6% average gain across both policy families in the real world, while adding only 2-3% to the parameter count. These results demonstrate that GeoProp is a simple yet high-impact inductive bias for generalist embodied policies. Project page: https://alibaba-damo-academy.github.io/GeoProp/.

AI.tldr: GeoProp is a lightweight adapter that aligns robotic proprioception with visual tokens through geometric grounding (projecting 3D kinematics onto 2D image planes, spatial feature sampling, and FiLM modulation) and short-horizon look-ahead prediction, improving manipulation policies like Diffusion Policy and pi_0 across 67 tasks with minimal parameter overhead (2-3%).
AI.motivation: Standard proprioception fusion methods treat robot state as an isolated vector lacking explicit alignment with visual tokens, causing manipulation policies to struggle grounding the robot's state within the scene and underperform even vision-only baselines.
AI.method: GeoProp projects robot state onto the image plane to sample localized visual features (grounded state token), injects state-derived spatial priors into visual features via FiLM modulation, and samples features at short-horizon predicted coordinates from recent kinematics for look-ahead visual context.
AI.result: Improves Diffusion Policy by 8.7% on 63 simulation tasks, pi_0 by 4.0% on RoboTwin subset, and yields 10.6% average gain across both policy families in real-world settings, with only 2-3% parameter increase.
AI.conclusion: GeoProp is a simple yet high-impact inductive bias for generalist embodied policies, demonstrating that explicit geometric grounding between proprioception and vision significantly improves robotic manipulation performance.

title: Physics-Audited Agentic Discovery in Scientific Machine Learning
summary: In agentic scientific machine learning (SciML), large language model (LLM) agents can discover surrogate models and select one by an automated score, typically an error metric. A low error, however, does not establish that the predicted fields satisfy the physics that matter for mechanics, such as boundary conditions, superposition, stiffness scaling, or causality. We introduce Physics-Audited Agentic SciML (PA-SciML), a verification-first workflow for agentic SciML discovery. The workflow fixes a scoring evaluator before search, derives reviewable machine-checkable physics requirements, checks each trained candidate on its outputs, and separately searches prescribed input ranges or measured load-history spans for high-violation cases without reference solution fields. A surrogate is reported as verified only under the stated checks. When enabled, the workflow also adds advisory numerical probes before training and tests one modeling change at a time to record which isolated edits are associated with score gains before reuse. In the reported computational-solid-mechanics numerical examples, the static elasticity run selects a surrogate with lower validation error than the error-only baseline while both selected models pass the common linear-elastic checks. In the transient elastodynamics run, an error-only baseline with similar mean error fails a stricter causality check by responding to future parts of the loading history, while the selected surrogate passes the stated checks. The main distinction is per-candidate physics evidence on predicted fields, not a richer aggregate score.

AI.tldr: PA-SciML introduces a verification-first workflow for agentic SciML that audits surrogate models against physics requirements (boundary conditions, superposition, stiffness scaling, causality) beyond standard error metrics, demonstrating that error-only baselines can pass physics-violating surrogates (e.g., acausal responses in elastodynamics) while the proposed method enforces per-candidate physics evidence.
AI.motivation: Standard error metrics in agentic SciML fail to guarantee that discovered surrogate models satisfy fundamental physics principles (boundary conditions, superposition, stiffness scaling, causality), risking deployment of physically invalid models despite low numerical error.
AI.method: PA-SciML: (1) fix a scoring evaluator before search; (2) derive reviewable machine-checkable physics requirements; (3) check each trained candidate on outputs; (4) separately search input/load-history spans for high-violation cases without reference solutions; (5) optionally add advisory numerical probes pre-training and test one modeling change at a time to isolate score-gain edits.
AI.result: Static elasticity: PA-SciML selects surrogate with lower validation error than error-only baseline, both passing linear-elastic checks. Transient elastodynamics: error-only baseline with similar mean error fails causality check (responds to future loading), while PA-SciML surrogate passes all stated checks.
AI.conclusion: The key distinction is per-candidate physics evidence on predicted fields rather than a richer aggregate score; physics auditing is essential for trustworthy surrogate discovery in mechanics.

title: Compositional Motion Generation from Demonstration with Object-Centric Neural Fields
comment: Accepted by IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RAL)
summary: Compositionality, by organizing complex behavior as combinations of simpler elements, enables robot learning that is scalable and data efficient. Leveraging this principle, we propose a generative learning-from-demonstration framework that enables compositional modeling of robotic behavior by connecting perception and motion through shared object-level representations. We render scenes from object-centric neural representations that integrate canonical neural fields with latent-conditioned deformations, capturing positional and geometric variations in a smooth, consistent, and interpretable way. For motion generation, a temporal mixture-of-experts (MoE) employs a gating mechanism to combine object-conditioned movement primitives over time, producing complete trajectories. This spatial-temporal compositionality maintains the data efficiency of movement primitives while grounding motion in visual structure, enabling systematic generalization across diverse scene configurations. In simulation, long-horizon manipulation tasks are successfully completed using the proposed model, which requires significantly less training data than other image-based baselines. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the method's robustness to noise, its ability to generalize at the category level through language-based segmentation models, and its capacity to operate directly on 3D scene representations.

AI.tldr: A generative LfD framework using compositional object-centric neural representations and temporal mixture-of-experts for data-efficient, generalizable robot manipulation.
AI.motivation: To achieve scalable and data-efficient robot learning by leveraging compositionality—organizing complex behavior as combinations of simpler elements—through connecting perception and motion via shared object-level representations.
AI.method: (1) Object-centric neural representations combining canonical neural fields with latent-conditioned deformations for smooth, interpretable scene rendering; (2) Temporal mixture-of-experts (MoE) with a gating mechanism that combines object-conditioned movement primitives over time to produce complete trajectories, enabling spatial-temporal compositionality.
AI.result: Outperforms image-based baselines with significantly less training data on long-horizon manipulation tasks in simulation; demonstrates robustness to noise, category-level generalization via language-based segmentation, and direct operation on 3D scene representations in real-world experiments.
AI.conclusion: Spatial-temporal compositionality via shared object-level representations maintains data efficiency of movement primitives while grounding motion in visual structure, enabling systematic generalization across diverse scene configurations.

title: MIRA-Math: A Benchmark for Minimal Information Requesting and Mathematical Reasoning
summary: Mathematical reasoning benchmarks typically provide all facts needed to solve each problem, while interactive benchmarks often mix reasoning with tools, retrieval, and long-horizon dialogue. We introduce MIRA-Math, a benchmark for a narrower diagnostic capability: solving mathematical problems whose full latent state has a unique answer, but whose solver-facing view is missing exactly one necessary atomic fact. The solver must request the missing information in natural language under a strict budget and then integrate the returned fact into an exact final answer. A fixed constrained LLM responder sees only the dataset-provided atomic fact and must either offer the quoted fact when the request matches it, or decline otherwise. Thus, instance generation, typed hint specifications, validation, and final-answer verification are deterministic, while request metrics are measured under a fixed LLM-mediated responder channel. MIRA-Math contains 2{,}310 generated instances from 22 typed mathematical families spanning algebra, probability, linear systems, discrete structures, signal processing, Markov chains, circuits, interpolation, and numerical boundary-value problems. Experiments across frontier and small models show that request success and final-answer accuracy are separable: models may ask for the right fact yet fail the downstream computation, or fail before obtaining the canonical hint. We release generators, verifiers, prompts, run metadata, and dataset documentation to support reproducible evaluation of minimal information requesting in mathematical reasoning.

AI.tldr: MIRA-Math is a benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning where each problem is missing exactly one atomic fact that the solver must request under a strict budget, then integrate into a final answer. It contains 2,310 instances across 22 mathematical families, showing that request success and final accuracy are separable capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing mathematical reasoning benchmarks provide all necessary facts upfront, while interactive benchmarks conflate reasoning with tools, retrieval, and dialogue. The authors aim to isolate and evaluate a narrower diagnostic capability: requesting a single missing atomic fact in natural language under a strict budget before solving a problem.
AI.method: The benchmark generates instances where each problem's full latent state has a unique answer, but the solver-facing view is missing exactly one necessary atomic fact. A fixed constrained LLM responder provides the fact only when the request matches; otherwise declines. Instance generation, hint specification, validation, and verification are deterministic. Request metrics are measured under a fixed LLM-mediated channel.
AI.result: Experiments across frontier and small models show that request success and final-answer accuracy are separable: models may successfully request the right fact yet fail downstream computation, or fail before obtaining the canonical hint.
AI.conclusion: MIRA-Math enables reproducible evaluation of minimal information requesting in mathematical reasoning, releasing generators, verifiers, prompts, run metadata, and dataset documentation.

title: Learning Spatiotemporal Tubes for Full Class of Signal Temporal Logic Tasks for Control of Unknown Systems under Input Constraints
summary: This paper presents a Spatiotemporal Tube (STT)-based control framework for general unknown nonlinear Euler-Lagrange (EL) systems subject to input constraints, with the objective of satisfying Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications, where confinement of the system trajectory within the STT guarantees the satisfaction of the corresponding STL task. For both single and multi-agent scenarios, the STT corresponding to each agent is modeled as a time-varying ball, whose center and radius are jointly parameterized using a physics-informed neural network (PINN). The robustness metric associated with the STL specification corresponding to the agents is incorporated into the training process as a loss function, enabling the learned tube to encode task-level temporal requirements. For a multi-agent scenario, we introduce an additional robustness metric corresponding to the global task, which, when satisfied, ensures the tubes do not collide with each other. To ensure that the system trajectory remains within the learned STT and thereby satisfies the local and global STL specifications, we propose a control strategy that explicitly accounts for input constraints. In particular, a closed-form control law is developed to keep the trajectory inside the tube while regulating the motion of the tube by enforcing bounds on its evolution depending on the input constraints of the system. The proposed approach has been validated over several case studies.

AI.tldr: A control framework using Spatiotemporal Tubes (STT) parameterized by physics-informed neural networks to enforce Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications for unknown nonlinear Euler-Lagrange systems under input constraints, with validated results in single and multi-agent scenarios.
AI.motivation: To enable unknown nonlinear Euler-Lagrange systems with input constraints to satisfy complex STL specifications, which are crucial for safety-critical autonomous systems but challenging due to system uncertainties and actuator limitations.
AI.method: (1) STT modeled as time-varying balls with center/radius parameterized by PINNs; (2) STL robustness metrics incorporated as loss functions for tube learning; (3) Additional global robustness metric for multi-agent collision avoidance; (4) Closed-form control law accounting for input constraints to keep trajectories within tubes.
AI.result: Validated over several case studies demonstrating the framework's effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed STT-PINN control framework successfully satisfies STL specifications under input constraints for both single and multi-agent EL systems, with formal guarantees through tube confinement.

title: Agentic Data Environments
summary:
Autonomous agents promise substantial gains in speed, scale, and labor efficiency, but their failures can impose abrupt and often irreversible costs. The central challenge for agentic automation is therefore to increase the benefits of automation while bounding the consequences of failure.
  While databases remain central to modern computing, agents operate over a broader data environment spanning files, APIs, applications, and system state. In this talk, I will outline early work on Agentic Data Environments -- the execution substrate in which agents operate -- that both amplify agent capabilities and enforce safety guarantees. This perspective reframes data systems from passive stores of state into active substrates for safe, reliable execution.

AI.tldr: This work proposes Agentic Data Environments as an execution substrate that reframes data systems from passive state stores into active platforms that both amplify agent capabilities and enforce safety guarantees, addressing the challenge of increasing automation benefits while bounding failure consequences.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents offer gains in speed, scale, and labor efficiency, but their failures can impose abrupt and irreversible costs. The central challenge is increasing automation benefits while bounding the consequences of failure.
AI.method: The paper outlines early work on Agentic Data Environments — the execution substrate in which agents operate — that spans files, APIs, applications, and system state. This reframes data systems from passive stores into active substrates for safe, reliable execution.
AI.result: Proposes that Agentic Data Environments both amplify agent capabilities and enforce safety guarantees simultaneously.
AI.conclusion: Data systems should be redesigned as active execution substrates rather than passive state stores, enabling agents to operate safely and reliably across broader data environments beyond traditional databases.

title: Disturbance-aware Motion Planning for Over-actuated Underwater Vehicles Exploiting Actuation Redundancy for High-fidelity 3D Reconstruction
summary: Underwater robots often operate near delicate targets where high-power thrusters resuspend sediments and induce turbulence, degrading image quality at the sensor input. Conventional controllers optimize vehicle-centric objectives, such as tracking and stability, without accounting for the impact of actuation on sensing. We address this actuation-to-perception coupling by exploiting redundancy in over-actuated platforms. For an eight-thruster ROV, multiple thrust allocations can yield the same motion; we search this null space to minimize predicted disturbance in a task-relevant target region while enforcing motion constraints. Our method uses a control-oriented thruster-wake proxy derived from actuator-disk theory with directional attenuation and validated by PIV ($R^2 = 0.99$ near the wake axis; $R^2 > 0.82$ in the primary wake region), together with a real-time redundancy-resolving allocator running at 10 Hz (45 ms/solve). Across 440 trials, the approach reduces target-region particle velocity by 67% ($p < 0.001$), improves 3D reconstruction RMSE by 55% versus a disturbance-unaware baseline ($1.9 \pm 0.4$ mm vs. $4.3 \pm 1.8$ mm), and achieves a 98.5% reconstruction success rate. The framework supports autonomous scanning, which is quantitatively evaluated, and operator-assisted inspection, which is demonstrated in the supplementary materials.

AI.tldr: A method that exploits thruster redundancy in over-actuated underwater robots to minimize flow disturbance in a target region, improving image quality and 3D reconstruction without compromising motion control.
AI.motivation: Underwater robots disturb sediments and create turbulence with high-power thrusters, degrading sensor input quality. Conventional controllers optimize vehicle-centric objectives (tracking, stability) but ignore how actuation impacts perception.
AI.method: Exploit redundancy in an eight-thruster ROV by searching the null space of thrust allocation to minimize predicted disturbance in a task-relevant target region while enforcing motion constraints. Uses a control-oriented thruster-wake proxy from actuator-disk theory with directional attenuation, validated by PIV, and a real-time redundancy-resolving allocator running at 10 Hz.
AI.result: 440 trials: 67% reduction in target-region particle velocity (p<0.001), 55% improvement in 3D reconstruction RMSE (1.9±0.4 mm vs. 4.3±1.8 mm), 98.5% reconstruction success rate.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively mitigates actuation-to-perception coupling in over-actuated underwater robots, supporting both autonomous scanning and operator-assisted inspection.

title: Reason Less, Verify More: Deterministic Gates Recover a Silent Policy-Violation Failure Mode in Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary:
Tool-using LLM agents can violate the very policies they are deployed to enforce while appearing to complete the task successfully. In policy-permissive environments, a tool may execute any well-formed call even when the corresponding state transition is forbidden by domain policy. The result is a silent wrong state (a booking cancelled, a passenger count changed, a claim acted on without verification) that neither the tool nor the agent's self-report exposes.
  We study this failure mode in the $τ^2$-bench airline domain. On a budget agent, 78% of observed failures are silent wrong-state failures with no tool error, and the aggregate failure rate is reproducible across disjoint seeds, not sampling noise. We then evaluate a lightweight intervention: deterministic, read-only pre-execution gates that inspect the proposed call and current state before allowing a write. A four-gate suite raises full-benchmark success from 29.6% to 42.0% on gpt-4o-mini (+12.4pp; paired task-level bootstrap P=0.0012), and the lift reproduces on a disjoint 15-seed set (+12.3pp; P=0.0008).
  The effect is concentrated where the gates fire: on the 26/50 firing tasks, success rises by +19.2pp, while movement on the 24 non-firing tasks does not exclude zero. Two negative controls (a self-enforcing retail domain and BFCL) bound the mechanism: gates help when tools are policy-permissive and add little where tools already self-enforce. As suggestive evidence, not a central claim, the same failure mode persists at the frontier: gpt-5.2 at default reasoning still attempts policy-violating writes, and the same suite improves success from 61.2% to 71.6% (+10.4pp; P=0.020; n=5, no replication). The contribution is a bounded evaluation and reliability result: deterministic gates do not guarantee task success, but they can deterministically prevent a known class of silent policy-violating writes at the action boundary.

AI.tldr: Tool-using LLM agents often produce silent wrong-state failures (e.g., booking cancellations, unauthorized changes) because tools execute any well-formed call even if it violates domain policy. In the τ²-bench airline domain, these failures account for 78% of observed errors. A lightweight intervention—deterministic, read-only pre-execution gates—reduces such failures, raising full-benchmark success from 29.6% to 42.0% on gpt-4o-mini (+12.4pp), with similar gains on a disjoint seed set (+12.3pp). Effects concentrate on firing tasks (+19.2pp) while non-firing tasks show near-zero improvement. Results are domain-specific: helpful where tools are policy-permissive, negligible where they self-enforce. The same failure mode persists even in frontier models (gpt-5.2), where the gates improve success from 61.2% to 71.6% (+10.4pp). The key contribution: deterministic gates cannot guarantee success but can deterministically prevent a known class of silent policy-violating writes at the action boundary.
AI.motivation: Tool-using LLM agents can silently violate the policies they are meant to enforce because tools execute any well-formed call regardless of whether the state transition violates domain policy, leading to undetected wrong states (e.g., cancelled bookings, unverified claims).
AI.method: The authors study this failure mode in the τ²-bench airline domain, measuring failure rates and types. They propose and evaluate a lightweight intervention: deterministic, read-only pre-execution gates that inspect the proposed call and current state before allowing a write operation. Experiments use gpt-4o-mini and gpt-5.2, with controls in a self-enforcing retail domain and BFCL.
AI.result: On a budget agent, 78% of observed failures are silent wrong-state failures without tool errors; the aggregate failure rate is reproducible across seeds. The four-gate suite raises full-benchmark success from 29.6% to 42.0% on gpt-4o-mini (+12.4pp; P=0.0012), replicated on a disjoint 15-seed set (+12.3pp; P=0.0008). On the 26/50 firing tasks, success rises by +19.2pp, while non-firing tasks show near-zero improvement. For gpt-5.2, success improves from 61.2% to 71.6% (+10.4pp; P=0.020; n=5, no replication).
AI.conclusion: Deterministic pre-execution gates do not guarantee task success, but they can deterministically prevent a known class of silent policy-violating writes at the action boundary. The mechanism is domain-dependent: helpful when tools are policy-permissive, less so when tools self-enforce.

title: Validate the Dream Before You Trust Its Verdict: Admissibility for World-Model Simulators
comment: Accepted at RSS 2026 Workshop on Robot World Models
summary: Across robotics, World Models (WMs) are increasingly used to evaluate action policies by simulating the consequences of actions in an imagined world, and returning a success or safety verdict. Yet a verdict is only as trustworthy as the WM that produced it, and the WM itself needs to be certified. In video-generation WMs, fidelity metrics such as Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) reward visual realism, but ignore whether the world responds correctly to the policy's actions, including those unseen in training. Classical simulation-based validation assumes a trusted simulator evaluating an untrusted policy, whereas generative WMs are themselves unverified learned artifacts. Hence, we argue that any WM used as a test oracle must first be accredited before its verdicts can serve as evidence. Building on credibility practices from safety-critical simulation, including Verification, Validation & Accreditation (VV&A), Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF), and scenario-based testing standards, we define an admissibility ladder (L0-L4) that a WM must climb before its closed-loop verdicts are accepted as assurance evidence. Our framework is embodiment-agnostic, and is instantiated in autonomous driving (AD), where assurance methods for traditional simulation are most mature. Applied to two driving WMs, the lower rungs reveal a reversal: the model that ranks higher on visual generation quality (L0) ranks lower on action-following (L1-L2), so visual fidelity does not predict the action-robustness a closed-loop verdict depends on.

AI.tldr: World Models used as test oracles for action policies require formal accreditation (via an admissibility ladder L0-L4) before their closed-loop verdicts can be trusted as evidence; visual fidelity (FVD) does not predict action-following robustness.
AI.motivation: World Models (WMs) are increasingly used to evaluate action policies by simulating action consequences and returning verdicts, but these verdicts are only as trustworthy as the WM that produced them. The WM itself is an unverified learned artifact, unlike classical simulation where the simulator is trusted. Therefore, WMs need to be certified or "accredited" before their outputs can serve as assurance evidence.
AI.method: The paper defines an embodiment-agnostic admissibility ladder (L0-L4) for accrediting World Models, building on credibility practices from safety-critical simulation: Verification, Validation & Accreditation (VV&A), Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF), and scenario-based testing standards. The framework is instantiated in autonomous driving (AD), applied to two driving WMs.
AI.result: Applied to two driving WMs, lower rungs reveal a reversal: the model that ranks higher on visual generation quality (L0) ranks lower on action-following (L1-L2). Visual fidelity does not predict the action-robustness that a closed-loop verdict depends on.
AI.conclusion: Any WM used as a test oracle must first be accredited before its verdicts can serve as evidence. The proposed admissibility ladder provides a structured approach, and the empirical reversal between visual fidelity and action-following underscores that accreditation must go beyond generation quality metrics.

title: InductWave: Inductive Multi-Hop Logical Query Answering on Knowledge Graphs
summary: Logical Multi-Hop Query Answering over Knowledge Graphs (KGs) can be formulated as querying, with an implicit completeness assumption. Current works mainly focus on Existential First Order Logic (EFO) queries. These EFO queries contain conjunction, disjunction, and negation operators. Most existing works employ transductive reasoning, meaning they are not capable of reasoning over entities unseen during training. In the real world, there is a resource scarcity, and we cannot train a model with all the nodes of a large KG. Hence, we propose InductWave, a wavelet-based inductive embedding method for logical query answering on large KGs. Here, the training graph consists of fewer nodes than the test graph. Our model performs on par with the baseline models while having half the number of message-passing layers. It outperforms all of them in most cases, with 75% of the layers. These fewer resource requirements enable us to evaluate InductWave on massive graphs, such as Wiki-KG. We test our model using extensive experiments across varying train-test graph proportions of the FB15k-(237) dataset, comparing it with the state-of-the-art models. The code and datasets for the model are available at https://github.com/kracr/inductwave/.

AI.tldr: InductWave is a wavelet-based inductive embedding method for logical multi-hop query answering over knowledge graphs that uses fewer message-passing layers (half to 75% of baselines) while achieving competitive or superior performance, enabling efficient reasoning on large KGs with unseen entities.
AI.motivation: Current transductive reasoning methods cannot handle unseen entities during inference, and training on all nodes of large KGs is resource-intensive. The authors aim to develop an inductive approach that requires fewer resources while maintaining performance.
AI.method: InductWave employs wavelet-based inductive embeddings for logical query answering, using fewer message-passing layers (half to 75% of baseline models) to achieve efficient reasoning over large knowledge graphs with unseen entities.
AI.result: InductWave performs on par with baselines using only half the message-passing layers, and outperforms all baselines in most cases with 75% of the layers. It also scales to massive graphs like Wiki-KG.
AI.conclusion: InductWave demonstrates that inductive reasoning with fewer layers is feasible and effective for logical multi-hop query answering on large KGs, addressing resource scarcity and unseen entity challenges.

title: Manual, Joystick, or Haptic Control? An In Vitro Comparison of Navigation Strategies for Robotic Interventional Neuroradiology Procedures
summary: Objective: To evaluate robotic controller interfaces for interventional neuroradiology procedures in-vitro incorporating a force-sensing platform to assess safety. Methods: A custom endovascular robot, device-mimicking controller, and sensorized neurovascular phantom were developed. Ten interventional neuroradiologists (4 novices, 6 experts) performed simulated navigations using four control modalities: device-mimicking controllers with and without haptic feedback, joystick-based input, and manual navigation. Navigation time, peak vessel-wall forces, incorrect catheterisations, and prolapse events were assessed, alongside user analyses. Results: Manual navigation was fastest (mean 47.7 s) compared to haptic-on (248.7 s), haptic-off (314.7 s), and joystick (392.6 s) modalities (p<0.001). Regardless of controller type, vessel-wall forces were below the 0.70 N puncture threshold; therefore all modalities were considered safe. Joystick produced significantly more prolapse events than manual control (1.56 vs 0.13; p=0.018). Operator experience was relevant to performance: experts made fewer incorrect catheterisations than novices (0.25 vs 0.62; p=0.035) and applied less vessel-wall force (p<0.0005); these effects were sustained across controllers but accentuated when haptics were on. Users perceived haptic on and haptic off as similarly intuitive, and more intuitive than joystick (p=0.033). Conclusion: Device-mimicking robotic controllers outperform joystick interfaces on most metrics; haptic feedback shows promising but non-significant performance benefits.

AI.tldr: A study comparing robotic controller interfaces for neurovascular interventions found that manual navigation was fastest, all modalities were safe (below 0.70N vessel-wall puncture threshold), device-mimicking controllers outperformed joystick interfaces, and haptic feedback showed promising but non-significant performance benefits.
AI.motivation: To evaluate the safety and performance of different robotic controller interfaces for interventional neuroradiology procedures using a force-sensing neurovascular phantom platform.
AI.method: Ten interventional neuroradiologists (4 novices, 6 experts) performed simulated navigations using four control modalities (device-mimicking controllers with/without haptic feedback, joystick, and manual navigation) in a custom endovascular robot with a sensorized neurovascular phantom. Navigation time, peak vessel-wall forces, incorrect catheterisations, and prolapse events were assessed.
AI.result: Manual navigation was fastest (47.7s vs 248.7-392.6s, p<0.001). All modalities were safe (<0.70N puncture threshold). Joystick produced more prolapse events than manual (1.56 vs 0.13, p=0.018). Experts outperformed novices in incorrect catheterisations (0.25 vs 0.62, p=0.035) and vessel-wall forces (p<0.0005). Device-mimicking controllers were perceived as more intuitive than joystick (p=0.033).
AI.conclusion: Device-mimicking robotic controllers outperform joystick interfaces on most metrics; haptic feedback shows promising but non-significant performance benefits for neurovascular interventions.

title: The Blind Curator: How a Biased Judge Silently Disables Skill Retirement in Self-Evolving Agents
summary: A self-evolving agent retires its bad skills by watching them fail, so what happens when the judge cannot see the failures? Skill retirement is the structural constraint that keeps a growing library from drifting below the no-skill baseline, but its guarantee assumes an unbiased reward, which is false for the LLM judges that reference-free tasks force upon us. We show that a biased judge does not merely add noise; it \emph{silently switches off the curator}. We make this precise with a corrupted-reward analysis and, isolating the causal channel by injecting corruption on top of a deterministic reward, a behavioral study on a reference-free report-writing testbed with a code-generation cross-check. Symmetric noise leaves retirement intact, but \emph{false-pass} bias (failures slipping through as passes) disables contribution-based retirement past a sharp threshold that no amount of data can cross. Separating genuine retirement from cap-eviction churn shows this \emph{mechanism} failure is universal, holding across domains and failure rates and sparing only near-zero-false-pass, verifier-like graders. The downstream \emph{outcome}, though, is regime-dependent: eval quality degrades only where the same corruption also starves skill synthesis, and otherwise holds steady, so the disabled curator is \emph{silent}, surfacing in no aggregate metric. The contribution is a behavioral safety result, not a performance one. A cheap defect-injection audit then tells an operator, before deployment, which side of the threshold their judge occupies.

AI.tldr: Biased LLM judges silently disable skill retirement in self-evolving agents, causing a mechanism failure that passes a sharp threshold uncorrectable by data; a defect-injection audit can detect this pre-deployment.
AI.motivation: Skill retirement in self-evolving agents assumes an unbiased reward signal, but reference-free tasks require LLM judges that are inherently biased, raising the question of whether such bias undermines the retirement mechanism beyond mere noise.
AI.method: The paper performs a corrupted-reward analysis and a behavioral study on a reference-free report-writing testbed with code-generation cross-check, injecting corruption on top of a deterministic reward to isolate causal channels. It also distinguishes genuine retirement from cap-eviction churn.
AI.result: False-pass bias (failures seen as passes) disables contribution-based retirement past a sharp, data-insurmountable threshold. This mechanism failure is universal across domains and failure rates, sparing only near-zero-false-pass verifier-like graders. The downstream eval quality degrades only when the same corruption also starves skill synthesis; otherwise, the failure is silent (no aggregate metric reflects it).
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a behavioral safety result (not a performance one) and proposes a cheap defect-injection audit to determine, before deployment, which side of the threshold a judge occupies.

title: Programmable Synchronization Graphs for Adaptive and Fault-Tolerant Modular Miniature Robots
summary: Modular miniature robots could provide scalable function in constrained environments, but coordinating many imperfect modules remains difficult when computation, communication and reliability are limited. A central robotics challenge is to coordinate many actuator-sensor modules without assigning a privileged leader, prescribing a fixed gait template, or relying on dense communication. Here we introduce a programmable synchronization-graph framework for modular miniature robots in which each actuator-sensor pair is represented as a network node and locomotor coordination is encoded through graph coupling. Fixed intra-subgraph links synchronize heterogeneous actuator groups, whereas a small number of signed inter-subgraph links program phase relationships between groups. In physical robot collectives with up to nine modules, graph coupling drives the emergence of synchronization, signed links tune the phase difference from in-phase to out-of-phase motion, and floor experiments produce gallop-like and trot-like contact patterns in a five-module robot assembly. Replacing dense all-to-all coupling with sparse d-regular topologies preserves synchronization while reducing the coupling burden. The same graph representation also captures fault tolerance: increasing graph degree increases the number of module deactivations tolerated before desynchronization. Finally, an upper-confidence-bound edge-selection algorithm learns inter-subgraph links that drive the system toward target phase states. In a separate deactivation benchmark, the graph-based controller avoids the leader-specific failure mode observed in centralized leader-follower control and reduces worst-case phase error by about threefold. These results establish programmable network topology as a compact control layer for gait phase programming, online adaptation and robustness to unit loss in modular miniature robots.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a programmable synchronization-graph framework for modular miniature robots, where actuator-sensor pairs serve as network nodes. Graph coupling enables synchronization, signed inter-subgraph links program phase relationships (e.g., gallop/trot gaits), sparse d-regular topologies reduce coupling burden, and an upper-confidence-bound algorithm learns target phase states. Graph-based control avoids leader-follower failure modes and reduces worst-case phase error by ~3×.
AI.motivation: Coordinating many imperfect, resource-constrained modular miniature robots remains difficult when computation, communication, and reliability are limited, and centralized leader-follower approaches suffer from single-point failures.
AI.method: A synchronization-graph framework where each actuator-sensor module is a node; fixed intra-subgraph links synchronize heterogeneous actuator groups; signed inter-subgraph links program phase offsets; sparse d-regular topologies replace dense all-to-all coupling; an upper-confidence-bound edge-selection algorithm learns inter-subgraph links for target phase states.
AI.result: Up to 9 modules demonstrated synchronization; signed links tuned phase differences; five-module assembly produced gallop-like and trot-like contact patterns; sparse coupling preserved synchronization; higher graph degree increased fault tolerance; UCB-based learning drove system to target phases; graph control avoided leader-specific failure and reduced worst-case phase error by ~3×.
AI.conclusion: Programmable network topology serves as a compact control layer for gait phase programming, online adaptation, and robustness to unit loss in modular miniature robots, offering advantages over centralized leader-follower approaches.

title: SpaCellAgent: A Self-Evolving LLM-Based Multi-Agent Framework for Trajectory Analysis
summary: Spatial and Single-cell transcriptomics are transformative in deciphering cellular dynamics. As the fundamental paradigm for reconstructing cell developmental paths, trajectory inference (TI) is critical. However, existing methods require extensive manual intervention and proficiency in heterogeneous tools, posing a significant barrier to efficient TI analysis. To bridge this gap, we propose SpaCellAgent, an autonomous large language model (LLM) multi-agent framework that automates end-to-end spatiotemporal analysis and narrative generation. SpaCellAgent utilizes a multi-agent architecture for strategic workflow planning, a dynamic tool-orchestration engine for adaptive algorithm selection, and a self-evolution module that iteratively refines performance through feedback. We evaluate SpaCellAgent on six heterogeneous datasets encompassing complex temporal developmental trajectories, diverse sequencing platforms, and spatially-resolved tissue architectures. SpaCellAgent consistently demonstrates over 40\% improvement in analytical efficiency while maintaining expert-aligned performance. By converting natural language specifications into optimized analytical workflows and fully automating the pipeline, SpaCellAgent democratizes advanced spatiotemporal modeling and establishes a scalable, agent-driven paradigm for computational biology. The code and materials are available at https://github.com/LittleXH-shw/SpaCellAgent.

AI.tldr: SpaCellAgent is an LLM multi-agent framework that automates end-to-end spatial and single-cell trajectory inference, achieving >40% efficiency improvement across six heterogeneous datasets while maintaining expert-aligned performance.
AI.motivation: Existing trajectory inference methods require extensive manual intervention and proficiency in heterogeneous tools, creating a significant barrier to efficient analysis.
AI.method: SpaCellAgent employs a multi-agent architecture for strategic workflow planning, a dynamic tool-orchestration engine for adaptive algorithm selection, and a self-evolution module for iterative refinement through feedback.
AI.result: Demonstrates over 40% improvement in analytical efficiency while maintaining expert-aligned performance on six heterogeneous datasets spanning temporal developmental trajectories, diverse sequencing platforms, and spatially-resolved tissue architectures.
AI.conclusion: SpaCellAgent democratizes advanced spatiotemporal modeling by converting natural language specifications into optimized analytical workflows, establishing a scalable, agent-driven paradigm for computational biology.

title: TouchWorld: A Predictive and Reactive Tactile Foundation Model for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Dexterous manipulation in everyday environments requires both anticipation and reaction: a robot must predict how contact should evolve while rapidly correcting local errors caused by slip, misalignment, unstable grasping, or force mismatch. Vision and language provide semantic and geometric guidance, but they cannot reliably reveal hidden contact states such as force, slip, and contact stability. Although tactile sensing exposes these physical cues, most existing policies treat touch as a low-frequency observation stream within a monolithic action model, coupling slow task reasoning, action generation, and fast contact feedback in a single loop. We introduce TouchWorld, a predictive-and-reactive tactile foundation model for dexterous manipulation. TouchWorld uses a hierarchical policy that separates vision-language subtask planning, tactile world-model prediction, visuo-tactile goal-conditioned action generation, and high-frequency tactile residual refinement. A High-Level Planning Layer produces executable subtasks and predicts tactile subgoals; a Visuo-Tactile Goal-Conditioned Policy generates nominal action chunks; and a Tactile-Conditioned Refinement Policy performs online residual correction using recent tactile and proprioceptive feedback. By using touch as both a predictive contact reference and a fast feedback signal, TouchWorld preserves the semantic generalization of vision-language-action policies while improving local contact adaptation. Across six long-horizon and contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks, TouchWorld achieves 65.0% success in the clean setting and 53.7% success under human perturbations, outperforming the strongest baseline by 15.7 and 18.5 percentage points, respectively.

AI.tldr: TouchWorld is a hierarchical tactile foundation model for dexterous manipulation that separates vision-language planning, tactile world-model prediction, goal-conditioned action generation, and high-frequency tactile residual refinement. It achieves 65.0% success (clean) and 53.7% (under perturbations), outperforming baselines by 15.7 and 18.5 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Existing policies treat tactile sensing as a low-frequency observation stream within a monolithic action model, coupling slow task reasoning, action generation, and fast contact feedback in a single loop — failing to handle the dual requirement of anticipation (predicting contact evolution) and reaction (correcting local errors like slip, misalignment, and force mismatch).
AI.method: TouchWorld employs a hierarchical policy with three layers: (1) High-Level Planning Layer — produces executable subtasks and predicts tactile subgoals using vision-language; (2) Visuo-Tactile Goal-Conditioned Policy — generates nominal action chunks; (3) Tactile-Conditioned Refinement Policy — performs online residual correction using recent tactile and proprioceptive feedback at high frequency.
AI.result: Across six long-horizon, contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks, TouchWorld achieves 65.0% success in clean settings and 53.7% success under human perturbations, outperforming the strongest baseline by 15.7 and 18.5 percentage points respectively.
AI.conclusion: By using touch as both a predictive contact reference (via world model) and a fast feedback signal (via residual refinement), TouchWorld preserves the semantic generalization of vision-language-action policies while significantly improving local contact adaptation.

title: Search, Fail, Recover: A Training Framework for Correction-Aware Reasoning
summary: Many reasoning tasks are not well described by a single left-to-right chain: a solver may need to pursue a plausible branch, observe delayed failure, and return to the latest prefix that can still be completed. We introduce Pyligent, a training and inference framework inspired by the Diligent Learner formulation that represents reasoning as validated search over partial solution chains. A task validator labels generated continuations and failures, and the resulting search trees are converted into supervised targets for three actions: continue, finish, and backtrack, with optional traces that summarize abandoned branches. We evaluate Pyligent on a hidden directed graph task designed to isolate delayed-failure recovery, and on structured reasoning domains with exact validators, including $4{\times}4$ Sudoku, Sudoku with reasoning traces, and Blocksworld. Compared with gold-only supervised fine-tuning, Pyligent improves solve rate by $72.7$ percentage points on hidden graphs, by $17$ and $18$ points on mixed and expert Sudoku, by $27$ and $14$ points on mixed and expert Sudoku with reasoning traces, and by $13$ points on Blocksworld. These results suggest that explicit failed-branch supervision can teach useful recovery behavior beyond imitation of polished solution chains.

AI.tldr: Pyligent is a training and inference framework that improves reasoning by explicitly supervising backtracking from failed branches, achieving large gains (up to ~73 percentage points) over standard fine-tuning on hidden graph, Sudoku, and Blocksworld tasks.
AI.motivation: Many reasoning tasks cannot be solved by a simple left-to-right chain; solvers need to backtrack from failed branches and recover, yet standard supervised fine-tuning only imitates successful solution chains and does not teach recovery behavior.
AI.method: Pyligent represents reasoning as validated search over partial solution chains. A task validator labels continuations and failures; search trees are converted into supervised targets for three actions (continue, finish, backtrack), with optional traces summarizing abandoned branches.
AI.result: Compared to gold-only SFT, Pyligent improves solve rate by 72.7 pp on hidden graphs, 17/18 pp on mixed/expert Sudoku, 27/14 pp on mixed/expert Sudoku with reasoning traces, and 13 pp on Blocksworld.
AI.conclusion: Explicit supervision on failed branches effectively teaches recovery behavior that imitation of polished solution chains alone cannot provide.

title: Multimodal Voice Activity Projection for Turn-Taking in Social Robots with Voice-Activity-Related Pretrained Encoders
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026). Acceptance notification date: 30 May 2026. Final published version pending
summary: Turn-taking prediction is a key requirement for social robots involved in human-human interaction, particularly in mediator settings, where the robot must anticipate conversational dynamics rather than merely react to pauses. This work presents a Multimodal Voice Activity Projection (MM-VAP) framework that extends the original audio-only VAP formulation to synchronized audio-visual inputs while preserving its self-supervised future-projection objective. The proposed approach builds on pretrained audio-visual backbones originally optimized for speech-related tasks and adapts them through Low-Rank Adaptation to the multimodal turn-taking problem. After independent speaker encoding, an inter-speaker attention stage models the relational dynamics required to project future voice activity. In addition, a semantic consistency loss is introduced to regularize the 256-state output space according to higher-level dialogue activity patterns. Experiments on NoXi and NoXi+J showed improvements over the current baselines, particularly for some turn-taking events. Additional evaluation on the Haru EDR corpus further supported the suitability of this direction for mediation-oriented human-robot interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MM-VAP, a multimodal framework extending audio-only Voice Activity Projection to synchronized audio-visual inputs for turn-taking prediction in social robot mediator settings. It uses pretrained audio-visual backbones adapted via Low-Rank Adaptation, inter-speaker attention for relational dynamics, and a semantic consistency loss. Evaluations on NoXi, NoXi+J, and Haru EDR corpora show improvements over baselines.
AI.motivation: Turn-taking prediction is critical for social robots mediating human-human interaction, but prior work largely relies on audio-only pause detection. Robots in mediator roles need to anticipate conversational dynamics proactively rather than reactively, motivating a multimodal approach that leverages both audio and visual cues.
AI.method: The MM-VAP framework extends audio-only VAP to audio-visual inputs using pretrained backbones (adapted via Low-Rank Adaptation), independent speaker encoding, inter-speaker attention for relational dynamics, and a semantic consistency loss to regularize the 256-state output space according to dialogue activity patterns.
AI.result: Experiments on NoXi, NoXi+J, and Haru EDR corpora demonstrate improvements over current baselines, particularly for certain turn-taking events, supporting the framework's effectiveness for mediation-oriented human-robot interaction.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multimodal approach to turn-taking prediction outperforms audio-only baselines, and the inclusion of visual modalities with LoRA adaptation and semantic consistency loss proves beneficial for social robots in mediator settings.

title: Do LLM-Generated Skills Make Better AI Data Scientists? A Component Ablation Across Data-Science Workflows
comment: KDD 2026 Workshop on AI Data Scientist
summary: Product data scientists often ask LLM-based agents to help with recurring execution tasks such as cleaning data, writing SQL, choosing statistical tests, and formatting results. Reusable skill files are meant to avoid prompting from scratch by packaging guidance for a task family. Expert-written skills can encode high-quality guidance, but writing and maintaining them across many data-science task families creates a manual bottleneck. We ask whether LLM-generated skills offer a useful low-curation alternative: do they improve performance over the task prompt alone? We test this question across four lifecycle stages: data preparation, data extraction, statistical analysis, and reporting, using one generated skill per stage. We find no reliable improvement from full generated skills over No-Skill prompting. We then ask whether any part of the skill is useful by ablating different skill components. The main ablation covers 56 tasks, nine model configurations, and three providers, yielding 7,560 runs. Compared with prompting using the task alone, neither the full generated skill nor any ablated skill variant significantly improves performance; all p-values are at least 0.396, and the total spread across variants is only 1.2 pp. A supplemental token-matched control adds 1,512 runs and finds that Full skills perform similarly to task-irrelevant skill-formatted content. The results caution against using one LLM-generated skill per data-science workflow as a default single-shot prompting strategy.

AI.tldr: LLM-generated skills for data science tasks do not improve performance over task-prompt-only baselines, as shown across 9,072 runs covering 56 tasks, nine model configurations, and three providers.
AI.motivation: Expert-written skill files can encode high-quality guidance for recurring data-science tasks, but maintaining them across many task families creates a manual bottleneck. The authors investigate whether LLM-generated skills can serve as a low-curation alternative.
AI.method: Tested across four lifecycle stages (data preparation, data extraction, statistical analysis, reporting) with one generated skill per stage. Conducted a large-scale ablation study covering 56 tasks, nine model configurations, three providers (7,560 runs), plus a token-matched control (1,512 runs).
AI.result: No reliable improvement from full generated skills over No-Skill prompting. All p-values ≥ 0.396, spread across variants only 1.2 pp. Full skills performed similarly to task-irrelevant skill-formatted content in token-matched control.
AI.conclusion: Using one LLM-generated skill per data-science workflow as a default single-shot prompting strategy is not beneficial; the approach does not improve performance over task-prompt-only baselines.

title: Towards Reliable Aerial Ground Vehicle Collaboration: An Integrated Planning and Autonomy Framework for Field Deployment
summary: Limited flight endurance significantly restricts the operational range of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in long duration missions such as surveillance and inspection, where multiple spatially distributed Areas of Interest (AOIs) must be visited. These tasks require efficient routing determining the sequence of visits which directly impacts mission time, energy consumption, and overall feasibility. Pairing UAVs with unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) for mobile recharging offers a promising solution, but introduces a tightly coupled cooperative routing problem involving UAV route planning, UGV road constrained movement, energy management, and rendezvous scheduling under uncertainty. In this work, we present an integrated planning and autonomy framework for reliable field deployment. We formulate the problem as an energy constrained cooperative routing task and solve it using a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) based planner that jointly optimizes the UAV visitation sequence and rendezvous locations with the UGV, outperforming baseline heuristics in minimizing total mission time. To bridge the gap between planning and execution, we introduce a standardized two layer YAML based mission API that captures environment states and structures lightweight, synchronized action sequences. This framework is supported by a complete autonomy stack using PX4/MAVSDK for UAV control and ROS 2/Nav2 for UGV navigation. Furthermore, we propose a lightweight Rendezvous Aware Replanner (RARP) that operates online to handle environmental uncertainties, reducing energy margin violations from 83.33% to 20.00%. The full system is validated through outdoor field experiments, demonstrating robust cooperative navigation and adaptability in dynamic tasks, including a search and rescue scenario with vision language model (VLM) based hazard detection

AI.tldr: The paper presents a DRL-based cooperative routing framework for UAV-UGV teams, where the UGV provides mobile recharging to extend UAV endurance. It includes a YAML-based mission API, a full autonomy stack (PX4/MAVSDK, ROS 2/Nav2), and an online Rendezvous Aware Replanner (RARP) that reduces energy margin violations from 83.33% to 20.00%. Field experiments validate the system in dynamic tasks including VLM-based hazard detection.
AI.motivation: Limited flight endurance restricts UAV operational range for long-duration missions (surveillance, inspection) involving multiple spatially distributed AOIs. Pairing UAVs with UGVs for mobile recharging introduces a tightly coupled cooperative routing problem that needs efficient joint optimization.
AI.method: Formulates energy-constrained cooperative routing as a DRL-based planner jointly optimizing UAV visitation sequence and rendezvous locations with UGV. Proposes a two-layer YAML-based mission API, integrates PX4/MAVSDK for UAV control and ROS 2/Nav2 for UGV navigation, and introduces RARP for online replanning under uncertainty.
AI.result: DRL planner outperforms baseline heuristics in minimizing total mission time. RARP reduces energy margin violations from 83.33% to 20.00%. Full system validated through outdoor field experiments.
AI.conclusion: The integrated planning and autonomy framework enables robust cooperative navigation and adaptability for UAV-UGV teams in dynamic real-world tasks, demonstrated in search and rescue with VLM-based hazard detection.

title: RL Post-Training Builds Compositional Reasoning Strategies
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Accepted to the 2nd Workshop on Compositional Learning at ICML 2026, Seoul, South Korea
summary: Does RL post-training merely amplify primitive skills already latent in a base model, or can it compose primitive skills into new higher-level strategies? We study this question in a fully observable rewrite-grammar environment where the pretraining distribution is known and every generated rewrite can be audited. A Transformer is pretrained on primitive symbol-rewrite chains and post-trained on a Trace-based reasoning task with only a binary final-answer reward. RL solves held-out problems that remain rarely solved by the pretrained model even under much larger sampling budgets, while rejection fine-tuning improves early but plateaus. Trace analysis shows that RL reorganizes primitive competence through a phased compositional mechanism: it first strengthens primitive reductions, then discovers valid composed procedures. These include sequential compositions, which collapse ordered chains of primitive contractions, and parallel compositions, which combine independent primitive contractions in a single step. The composed procedures are not isolated samples; they are reused and consolidated into a stable repertoire. Comparing RL with rejection fine-tuning shows that the key difference is not exploration volume but selectivity: RFT produces many shortcut-like rewrites, much of them invalid, whereas RL concentrates exploration into valid reusable structure. Pretraining ablations show that the emergence of compositional strategies is gated not by primitive exposure alone, but by whether pretraining organizes primitive competence into reduction procedures that RL can later compress. The base model provides weak procedural ingredients; RL builds them into reliable higher-level strategies.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether RL post-training can compose primitive skills into higher-level strategies beyond simply amplifying latent abilities. Using a rewrite-grammar environment with full observability, the authors show that RL discovers and consolidates compositional procedures (sequential and parallel) that the base model cannot achieve even with massive sampling, while rejection fine-tuning (RFT) plateaus due to invalid shortcuts. The key factor is RL's selective exploration, not volume, and the emergence of composition depends on pretraining organizing primitives into compressible reduction procedures.
